clue.text: Cargo packer has done time, they say

indicators.note: they say tells us the phrase is spoken and its sound gives a differently spelt word

parts.note: to have done time is to have served an age, so the phrase is heard as 'done age'

explanation.surface: Someone who loads cargo turns out to be an ex-convict, by all accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'they say' marks a homophone: 'done age' (served time) sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Dunnage is the loose packing material wedged among cargo in a ship's hold to stop it shifting.

clue.text: Bird table where waders not wanted

parts.note: a duck is a bird
a board is a table, as in 'bed and board'

explanation.surface: A bird table where long-legged birds are unwelcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waders' looks like birds but means waterproof boots: duckboards are laid over mud so you need none.
explanation.definitionFit: Duckboards are slatted planks laid over wet ground, so walkers stay dry without boots.

clue.text: Poor Venetian's endless simplicity

indicators.note: poor means badly made, so the letters are rearranged
endless says the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive adding no letter

explanation.surface: A poor Venetian leads a simple life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' drops the last N of VENETIAN to leave VENETIA, and 'Poor' rearranges that.
explanation.definitionFit: Naivete is innocent artlessness, a lack of worldly sophistication.

clue.text: Accommodation for servants in an equal race

parts.note: an gives the single letter A
par means equal, as in 'on a par'

indicators.note: in puts the servants inside the race

parts.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
men are servants, as in 'masters and men'

explanation.surface: Servants' quarters provided in a race of equals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal; the race is the Isle of Man TT, a famous motorcycle event, and 'servants' recalls the old phrase 'masters and men'.
explanation.definitionFit: An apartment is a set of rooms, a dwelling or lodging.

clue.text: Behold I Zingari, for example, in the middle of Greece!

indicators.note: in places the club's letters inside the centre of Greece
the middle of picks the central two letters of Greece

parts.note: I Zingari is a famous wandering amateur cricket club, so a CC (cricket club)

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a touring team in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: I Zingari is a famous English amateur cricket club, so it gives the abbreviation for cricket club; 'in' places it inside the two central letters picked by 'the middle of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecce is Latin for 'see!' or 'lo!', as in Ecce Homo.

clue.text: Pleiades at first, then the Plough, in the fable

indicators.note: at first asks for only the opening letter of the star-cluster name Pleiades

parts.note: arable land is land fit for the plough, so the Plough stands for arable

explanation.surface: A myth that starts with one constellation and moves on to another.
explanation.walkthrough: The Plough looks like a constellation alongside the Pleiades, but it stands for ARABLE, land that is ploughed.
explanation.definitionFit: A parable is a short moral story, much like a fable.

clue.text: To rub out on this MS was perhaps simple in the past

definitions.text: To rub out on this MS

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters could be put another way

explanation.surface: An old manuscript scraped clean so it could be written on again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals an anagram of SIMPLE and PAST.
explanation.definitionFit: A palimpsest is a parchment scraped of its writing and reused.

clue.text: Pass rope through the beak once

explanation.surface: Threading a rope through a bird's bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beak' is slang for a magistrate; a reeve was a medieval local official.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors reeve a line through a block or ring, and a reeve was an old official like a magistrate.

clue.text: Recall little woman in kindergarten originally

parts.note: Beth is one of the March sisters in Little Women

indicators.note: originally asks for the opening letter of kindergarten

explanation.surface: Remembering a small girl at nursery school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little woman' refers to Beth March of Louisa May Alcott's Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: To bethink oneself is to remember or think back.

clue.text: Join Everest leader on desolate climb

indicators.note: leader asks for the first letter of Everest
climb in a down clue means the word is read upwards, from the bottom

parts.note: lorn means lonely and desolate

explanation.surface: Sign up for an Everest expedition on a bleak ascent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climb' reverses the word for desolate in a down entry, so it reads upward from the bottom of the light.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol is to sign up as a member.

clue.text: Country dishes

explanation.surface: Food from a particular nation.
explanation.definitionFit: China is a nation in Asia, and china is also porcelain crockery such as plates and cups.

clue.text: He has a district to administer, he gathers

definitions.text: He has a district to administer

explanation.surface: An official runs his area and brings things in.
explanation.walkthrough: In British India a Collector was the chief officer in charge of a district.
explanation.definitionFit: A district officer in India held that title, and anyone who amasses stamps, coins or taxes is likewise one who gathers.

clue.text: You have to be quick to draw this

definitions.text: You have to be quick to draw this

parts.words: You have to be quick to draw this
parts.note: quick here means alive, not fast: only the living can draw air into the lungs, while the surface suggests a gunfighter's speed

explanation.surface: Advice about a fast draw, as in a gunfight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quick' is the old sense, living, as in 'the quick and the dead'.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhaling air is something only a living creature does, so a quick (alive) person can draw it.

clue.text: Majestic, like the White Queen's kitten

explanation.surface: A royal-looking pet in Lewis Carroll's Looking-Glass world.
explanation.walkthrough: In Through the Looking-Glass the White Queen turns out to be Alice's white kitten, so that kitten is in effect a queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Imperial means regal or befitting an emperor, and a kitten that was a queen is royal in that sense.

clue.text: Ugly ball he hit for six, showing profound amusement

indicators.note: hit for six means knocked about thoroughly, so the letters are scattered

explanation.surface: Someone smashes an awful delivery for six, to great hilarity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit for six' (a cricket term for a big hit over the boundary) signals an anagram of UGLY BALL HE.
explanation.definitionFit: A belly laugh is a deep hearty laugh.

clue.text: Bare teeth showing a sharp edge

indicators.note: showing says the letters are on display within the words Bare teeth

explanation.surface: A snarling animal reveals its teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'showing' tells you the answer is on view inside 'Bare teeth'.
explanation.definitionFit: An arete is a sharp mountain ridge, a knife-edge of rock.

clue.text: One of the quartets, by George! No. by Tom!

definitions.text: One of the quartets, by George! No. by Tom!

parts.words: One of the quartets, by George! No. by Tom!
parts.note: the Four Quartets are poems by an Eliot, not the novelist George Eliot but Tom, that is Thomas Stearns Eliot; 'by George' also poses as an exclamation

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims about a quartet, then corrects themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by George!' reads as an oath, but it names George Eliot; the correction 'by Tom!' points to T. S. Eliot, who wrote Four Quartets.
explanation.definitionFit: East Coker is the second of T. S. Eliot's Four Quartets, named after a Somerset village.

clue.text: Left a large fortune, TUC is in healthy state

parts.note: TUC is CUT written upwards in this down entry, so the letters say 'cut up'
being well is a healthy state

explanation.surface: Trade unions in good shape and leaving a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: TUC is the Trades Union Congress in the surface. In a down clue CUT read upward gives TUC.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut up well is an old idiom for leaving a large estate when you die.

clue.text: Continuing noise about boy getting the cane wrongly

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a son is a boy

indicators.note: wrongly says the letters of cane are set down in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A boy is unjustly caned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrongly' rearranges CANE into ANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Resonance is sound that lingers or reverberates.

clue.text: Poison in the finger of an Arab

parts.note: a finger is a digit
Ali is a typical Arab name, so 'of an Arab' is Ali's

explanation.surface: Something toxic on an Arab's hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Digitalis is a drug made from foxglove, toxic in all but small doses.

clue.text: Market gardener keeps a pound for the cab

indicators.note: keeps means holds inside, so the pound goes within the gardener

parts.note: a market gardener is a grower
L stands for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A grower saves money for a taxi.
explanation.walkthrough: A growler was a Victorian four-wheeled horse-drawn cab.
explanation.definitionFit: A growler was slang for a four-wheeled hackney carriage, so a kind of cab.

clue.text: Drinks like fish

explanation.surface: Someone who drinks heavily, as the saying goes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls 'drinks like a fish'; to tope is to drink to excess, and the tope is also a small shark.
explanation.definitionFit: To tope is to booze habitually, and a tope is a small shark, a kind of fish.

clue.text: Urge to take up exercise

parts.note: to press is to urge

explanation.surface: Encouragement to take up a fitness routine.
explanation.definitionFit: A press-up is a floor exercise lifting the body with the arms.

clue.text: Sound 'iding place in Anouilh's drama

indicators.note: Sound says the phrase is spoken aloud, giving a word spelt differently

parts.note: a glory hole is a cupboard where things are stashed out of sight; with the h dropped it is said 'glory 'ole'

explanation.surface: A hiding place in a French play, said in a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped H of ''iding' hints at Cockney 'glory 'ole'. Anouilh's plays L'Alouette (Joan of Arc) and Becket centre on saints, who wear a halo.
explanation.definitionFit: A gloriole is a halo, the ring of light around a saint such as Joan of Arc in Anouilh's play.

clue.text: Barometer for schooner

explanation.surface: Swapping a weather instrument for a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: A schooner is a ship, but also a tall drinking vessel for sherry or beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A barometer is called a glass in weather lore, and a schooner is a drinking vessel.

clue.text: First person to take legal action about second edition

parts.note: I is the first person singular pronoun

indicators.note: about means around, so the action word wraps the second

parts.note: to sue is to take legal action

explanation.surface: The first person to sue over a second edition.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is one printing of a magazine or newspaper.

clue.text: Organ showing malice

explanation.surface: A body part revealing ill will.
explanation.definitionFit: The spleen is an abdominal organ, once thought the seat of bad temper, hence spite.

clue.text: Flower spike, say

indicators.note: say tells us the word is spoken, giving a different spelling

parts.note: a tine is a spike or prong

explanation.surface: A plant's spike, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' looks like a bloom but means something that flows: the Tyne is a river in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tyne is a river, and a river is a thing that flows.

clue.text: Suitable place for a I dn to sit?

definitions.text: Suitable place for a I dn to sit?

parts.words: Suitable place for a I dn to sit?
parts.note: the cross-reference leads to a bird, the duck; a famous breed of duck shares its name with a town that is a parliamentary seat, so a duck could sit for it

explanation.surface: Where should the bird from another clue perch?
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is to 1 down, whose first part is DUCK. 'sit' means sitting in Parliament: Aylesbury is a Buckinghamshire town and constituency, and also a breed of white duck.
explanation.definitionFit: Aylesbury is a breed of domestic duck and a Commons constituency, so such a duck could be its member.

clue.text: No W German city has these other points

parts.note: the compass points apart from W are E, S and N
S is the compass point south
S again, south
E again, east
N, north

explanation.surface: A German city boasting no W, only the other letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No W ... these other points' says the city's name is built only from compass points other than W: E, S, S, E, N.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr, formerly in West Germany.

clue.text: The sort 'of noise made in creches

indicators.note: made in says the answer is fashioned out of the letters of creches

explanation.surface: Nurseries are full of shrill racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made in' signals an anagram of CRECHES.
explanation.definitionFit: A screech is a shrill piercing cry, the kind of noise toddlers make.

clue.text: The shine is off if the Oval's first 50 becomes a' century

indicators.note: the first L, the Roman numeral for 50, is swapped for C, the Roman hundred

parts.note: an oval is an ellipse

explanation.surface: A cricket score at the Oval turns from fifty into a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like cricket at the Oval, a London cricket ground, but the oval is an ELLIPSE whose first L (50) becomes C (100).
explanation.definitionFit: During an eclipse the sun's light is blocked, so its brightness disappears.
